entries.title: Cubs, Happ looking to snap out of recent hitting funk
entries.summary: <p>ATLANTA — The Cubs have one hit in their last 28 chances batting with runners in scoring position. They’ve scored three runs in their last four games entering play here Thursday night against the Braves. Collectively, they have 13 hits in 120 at-bats in that span, a batting average of .108.</p><p>Surely, even the most jaded denizen of Wrigleyville doesn’t expect this to go on indefinitely, although if you’re looking to break a slump, you wouldn’t nominate <b>Chris Sale</b> as the guy you’d most like to see looming over you on the mound.</p><p>Sale is a decade removed from the days when he was dealing for the White Sox, but since reviving his career three years ago when he came to Atlanta, he’s been as intimidating as ever, still throwing his fastball at 98 miles an hour. The left-hander won a Cy Young Award in 2024, was averaging just under 12 strikeouts per nine innings last season until fracturing a rib cage and missing 62 games, and at age 37 is off to another great start this season. He brought a 6-2 record, 2.20 ERA and 56 strikeouts in 49 innings into Thursday’s series finale against the Cubs.</p><p>“Yeah, he’s one of the best in the game, so it’ll be a good test for us,’’ left fielder <b>Ian Happ </b>said.</p><p>A test much better taken, it would seem, when the Cubs were scoring five or more runs a game, as they’ve done 23 times this season, including their last three games at home before this downturn.</p><p>The batting averages through the first 14 days of the month reflect the extent of the recent struggles. <b>Moises Ballesteros </b>is 2 for 34 (.059). <b>Seiya Suzuki </b>(.179), <b>Alex Bregman </b>(.209), Happ (.211), <b>Nico Hoerner </b>(.214), <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong </b>(.220). Even the team’s best-hitting regular in May, <b>Michael Busch </b>(.342), has been held hitless in Atlanta (0 for 5), though he has drawn three walks.</p><p>“We’ve run up high pitch counts, we’ve had traffic [on the bases}, the last few games we’re just not pushing it across, you know, all up and down the lineup, struggling to just push across the runs,’’ Happ said.</p><p>“But that happens over the course of a season. You’ll have a stretch where you get guys in scoring position, but you can’t quite get it done.’’</p><p>On Sunday, Happ’s streak of reaching base ended at 30 games. But during the last four games, he has struck out nine times in 11 at-bats.</p><p>“It felt like we were scoring six, seven runs a night [during the 10-game winning streak that ended Saturday], adding on the whole time,’’ he said. “But that’s baseball.</p><p>“Tonight, a good test. A good way to finish the series.’’</p><p><b>Amaya back in lineup</b></p><p>Catcher <b>Miguel Amaya</b>, who had complained of some back tightness Friday and hadn’t played in a week, was back in the starting lineup Thursday.</p><p>With left-hander Sale on the mound, manager <b>Craig Counsell </b>installed <b>Matt Shaw </b>in right field and Suzuki served as DH.</p><p><b>Bregman,</b> who homered Monday night and had two singles Tuesday night, moved up a spot in the order, batting second. Bregman started the season in the 2-spot but hadn’t hit there since April 26, with Ballesteros<b> </b>getting the majority of starts there.</p><p><b>Schedule updates</b></p><p>The Cubs announced a change in starting times for two games, one on the road, the second at home. The Memorial Day game (May 25) against the Pirates, originally scheduled to be a night game, is now scheduled for a 12:35 start. The start time of the Cubs’ game on Sunday night, June 7 at home against the Giants has been pushed back 10 minutes, to 7:30 p.m.<br></p>

entries.title: Man shot while getting out of his car in North Pullman
entries.summary: <p>A man was shot in North Pullman Thursday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 29, was getting out of his car in the 700 block of 103rd Street at 9:08 p.m. when someone shot at him, police said. He was hit in the head and taken to University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition.</p><p>No one in custody.</p>

entries.title: White Sox win fifth straight to break .500 for first time since end of 2022
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox have won five games in a row, and slugger Munetaka Murakami didn’t homer or drive in a run in any of them.</p><p>That’s how well things are going for the Sox (22-21), who beat the Royals 6-2 on Thursday night to move above .500 after 40-plus games for the first time since the penultimate game of the 2022 season, when they were 81-80.</p><p>While Murakami is mired in a 2-for-18 rut (with six walks) during the Sox’ run, others are providing the pop. On Thursday, it was Randal Grichuk, who went 2-for-3 with four RBI, including a two-run homer in the first that wiped out a 1-0 deficit. It was his third homer in eight games with the Sox, who signed the 13-year veteran May 4.</p><p>“He can really do damage against lefties,” manager Will Venable said. “It’s nice to be able to go find that midseason. He’s been doing it for a long time. We were really excited to be able to get him when [outfielder Austin] Hays went down. For us to grab that guy, it’s huge.”</p><p>With two outs in the first, Royals left-hander Kris Bubic walked Murakami. Then Grichuk hit a 2-2 pitch 401 feet to center field. In the third, Grichuk faced Bubic with the bases loaded and lined a two-run single to center.</p><p>“I know I’ve hit well against lefties, and that’s something I haven’t wavered from,” Grichuk said. “The results might not [always] be there, but the at-bats and the barrels are still there. So I go in with confidence knowing that that’s what I’m here for, and hopefully the results [follow].”</p><p>Sox lefty Anthony Kay threw a career-high six innings for his first quality start in 14 career starts. He lasted one batter into the seventh, when Kyle Isbel’s triple ended his day. After using righty Tyler Davis for six batters and lefty Sean Newcomb for four Wednesday, Venable went back to them. Davis completed the seventh, and Newcome closed it out for his first save of the season.</p><p>Next up on the nine-game homestand are the Cubs, who will help fill Rate Field and supercharge the atmosphere all weekend.</p><p>“I love playing against the Cubs,” said Grichuk, who faced them as part of another rivalry with the Cardinals in 2014-17, his first years in the majors. “They have a great fan base. They bring the energy. Hopefully, our fans come out and yell for us. Those are always fun games.”<br></p>

entries.title: Sorry, Bears fans: At least one handicapper sees fewer wins this season
entries.summary: <p>LAS VEGAS — Kiev O’Neil approaches sports betting surgically, like a cold, calculating assassin. Emotionless. So Bears fans might want to stop reading.</p><p>That he is a lifetime Bears fan might be the curveball of this equation because he is lying in wait to let the public inflate this very public franchise.</p><p>At the proper moment, he’ll strike, betting under a win total that he hopes climbs above 9½.</p><p>O’Neil operates The Odds Breakers out of Arizona. Every mid-April, he releases custom NFL Pythagorean win figures, comparing them to how many games each team won and using them to polish predictive analyses.</p><p>Rookie coach Ben Johnson and the Bears went 11-6 last season, winning the NFC North and beating the Packers in the playoffs. A divisional-round overtime home loss to the Rams served as the season-ending stinger.</p><p>The Bears had a preseason 8½ win total, pleasing all over bettors.</p><p>Last month, Las Vegas sportsbooks opened the Bears’ 2026 win total at 9½. William Hill posted under 9½ at -115. On Monday, Circa Sports had over 9½ at +100, under -120, or risk $120 to win $100.</p><p>BetMGM, which O’Neil can’t access in Arizona, offers adjusted win totals, -210 for Bears under 10½; -125 under 9½.</p><p>“I wait [to bet] the public teams,” O’Neil said. “Wait or don’t take at all.”</p><p>He can refer to the Bears as just another public team because his “Pythag” for them is 8.04, a -2.96 discrepancy to what occurred (11 wins) that’s the largest letdown of the 32 teams.</p><p>“I want 10 as my number,” O’Neil said. “I think their most likely outcome is nine wins, but there’s a chance they get to 10. My ‘Pythag’ says to go under, so that’s what I’m looking for.”</p><p>If an amped public boosts the Bears to 10½?</p><p>“If it gets to 10½, I’ll lay -200,” he said. “I’m in.”</p><p><b>K.C. fortunes fizzle</b></p><p>A year ago, O’Neil’s “Pythag” numbers steered him toward an under wager on the Chiefs’ 11½ win total. He bet on a regression to the mean that finally occurred for the team that had experienced great fortune since 2019.</p><p>Two seasons ago, Kansas City went 15-1 before a 38-0 thrashing at Denver.</p><p>One year ago, O’Neil concocted a “Pythag” figure of 9.80 for the Chiefs.</p><p>“Last year, Kansas City was literally the biggest discrepancy [of -5.2] I’d ever seen, from true actual wins to a ‘Pythag’ win total,” he said. “And they tanked that last game. They could have had 16 wins!”</p><p>To turn that huge 5.2 discrepancy into a mammoth 6.2.</p><p>“Massive regression coming,” O’Neil told me one year ago, “with an aging team.”</p><p>The Chiefs went 6-11 last season. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes, who suffered a season-ending knee injury, went 6-8 as a starter, dropping five of his last six games.</p><p>“That became my best under bet,’’ O’Neil said. ‘‘Among other things, the AFC West was getting stronger, better coaches were getting hired in that division, all making it a sure bet to the under.</p><p>“Whether it hits or not, the percentage of hitting it [was] higher than many others.”</p><p>The Chiefs’ win total this season is 10½, under -130, which I have already bet. That old team has only aged, and O’Neil established a 9.57 “Pythag” for Kansas City, confirming my decision.</p><p><b>Likes being right</b></p><p>O’Neil was raised in Downers Grove and went to Wisconsin in Madison. Those details were pertinent in the second week of January, when family and 30 close friends celebrated his 50th birthday in Puerto Vallarta.</p><p>On that certain Saturday night, the Bears once again trailed the Packers for three quarters before rallying in the fourth for the playoff triumph.</p><p>“There were about 20 Packers fans there,” he said. “A miserable first three quarters. The end? Pure joy. The biggest birthday present I could have gotten.”</p><p>As a fan.</p><p>As a gambler, he’s ruthless.</p><p>“You cannot expect the Bears to keep doing this unless [they] massively improve. This was clearly the luckiest team.”</p><p>The Bears’ plus-22 turnover differential led the NFL.</p><p>With those fourth-quarter cardiac comebacks in mind, O’Neil suggested it might be wise, at least for the first few games this year, to make first-half wagers against the Bears.</p><p>Fans could still bet on them for the game or wait till they trail to make moneyline bets that they’ll wake up, rally and win.</p><p>Those who did so in those two Packers games could have fetched about 10-to-1 odds in both cases.</p><p>O’Neil has discussed wagering with people who cannot bet against their team:</p><p>“I tell them, ‘You should bet on your team or against your team because that’s usually the team you know best.’ You have to completely separate the fact that you like them.</p><p>“Emotions never should be involved in sports betting. Otherwise, it’s just not for you, anyway.”</p><p>His “Pythags” have directed him to bet Giants over 7½ (+105) and Titans under 6½ (+115).</p><p>Six years ago, the company that produced “Pythags” went under. That spurred O’Neil to produce his own figures with advanced (or truer) exponents.</p><p>He recommends using these to complement approaches, such as gauging a fourth-place team now playing a first-place schedule, the draft, trades and coaching changes.</p><p>Visit his site to marvel at the mathematical details.</p><p>“It isn’t always just about the money you win; it’s about the glorification of just being right,” he said. “I like being right.”<br></p>

entries.title: Braves skipper Walt Weiss has fond memories of Craig Counsell, Dansby Swanson
entries.summary: <p>ATLANTA — Sure, Braves manager Walt Weiss said while standing behind the batting cage in Truist Park Thursday afternoon. He remembers the first time he met <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> manager Craig Counsell.</p><p>Weiss was the Colorado Rockies starting shortstop. Counsell was the 11th-round draft pick out of Notre Dame, in his first big-league camp. This was 30-plus years ago.</p><p>“I felt like I was looking in the mirror a little bit when he got to the big leagues,’’ Weiss said, smiling at the memory.</p><p>“He was a young me. I kind of took him under my wing. I took a liking to him right away when he was a kid.’’</p><p>The day before, Counsell had told reporters that Weiss used to buy him breakfast, back when they didn’t serve food to the players in spring training.</p><p>“He’s a good one, man,’’ Weiss said.</p><p>Future manager material?</p><p>“You never look at a young player in those terms for the most part,’’ Weiss said. “But he had a lot of stuff in order, you know. He was disciplined, he had work ethic. There was a high baseball IQ. So you look back now, and yeah, he had all the elements.’’</p><p>And now here they were, in opposing dugouts, as managers of the two teams with the best records in the National League. Weiss, who had come to peace with the possibility that he might not get another shot at managing after four years as Rockies manager, guiding the Braves to a 30-14 record, the first team in the majors to reach 30 wins.</p><p>Counsell, whCounsell, whose team this season already has had two 10-game winning streaks, broke a four-game losing streak with a 2-0 victory Thursday against Weiss and Atlanta.</p><p>Weiss was promoted from bench coach after Brian Snitker, the team’s previous manager and Bobby Cox disciple, took a senior advisory role. Alex Anthopoulos, the team’s president of baseball operations, placed a call to Weiss.</p><p>“I got my juices flowing once he asked me,’’ Weiss said, “and I started thinking about doing it here. Yeah, I really wanted to get that job. I knew the team so well, I’m so emotionally attached.’’</p><p>Weiss is well aware of how good the Cubs are, especially on defense.</p><p>“The cliche about [strength] up the middle, right?” Weiss said. “That guy in center field (Pete Crow-Armstrong) is a game-changer. I’ve known Dansby (Swanson) for a long time. We had him here for years. Nico (Hoerner). I love the guy.</p><p>“[The defense] is part of the reason [the Cubs] are going to be tough to deal with. It goes hand in hand with the run prevention thing, defense and good pitching.</p><p>“We’re a good defensive team, too. That’s why it would be a great matchup in October, if we get there.’’</p><p>Weiss tells the story of an early conversation with Swanson, who came to the Braves as the No. 1 overall pick in the draft.</p><p>“This was my first year with the Braves,’’ Weiss said. “I was the bench coach. He was a young shortstop. We were in the outfield, in Orlando, Disney [where the Braves trained], and he was a 1-1 pick, there was a lot of hype, people were saying he wasn’t really a 1-1.</p><p>“He’s finding his way as a young player in this league and had some struggles, and he was dealing with that.</p><p>“And I told him, ‘Dansby the only thing that matters is whether or not we can win a championship with you as our shortstop. Nothing else matters. That’s how you judge yourself.’’’</p><p>Three years later, in 2021, the Braves won the World Series. In the postgame jubilation on the field, Swanson found Weiss.</p><p>“We won a championship with me at short,’’ he said.</p><p>“He remembered that conversation,’’ Weiss said. “I still get goosebumps telling that story.’’</p><p>Swanson is still looking for his first championship in Chicago. entries.title: Illinois native — and Cubs draft pick — Bryan Hudson on a roll out of White Sox' bullpen
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> left-handed reliever Bryan Hudson was a pretty big deal as a prospect before the 2015 MLB Draft — and not just because of his 6-8 frame.</p><p>Though MLB.com ranked him as the 71st prospect, then-Cubs president Theo Epstein personally scouted Hudson when he pitched for Alton (Illinois) High School. Hudson never met Epstein, but he heard Epstein was at the game.</p><p>The Cubs ended up drafting Hudson in the third round on the recommendation of the late, great area scout Stan Zielinski, who also signed Kyle Schwarber and Jeff Samardzija, among many others, in his 38 years of scouting.</p><p>But after pitching at every level in the Cubs’ system, Hudson was let go in November 2022. To this day, he doesn’t understand what went wrong. He eventually landed with the Brewers and had an impressive 2024, but he couldn’t duplicate it in 2025 and was waived.</p><p>Enter the White Sox, who claimed him last year before trading him to the Mets for cash and then reacquiring him when the Mets waived him. Now, more than 10 years after being drafted, the 29-year-old Hudson entered the game Thursday against the Royals on a career-best run.</p><p>He hadn’t allowed a run in 17⅔ innings, spanning 19 outings. His 19-game scoreless streak was the longest by a Sox pitcher since Matt Albers went a franchise-record 30 in a row over the 2015 and ’16 seasons. The Sox’ longest single-season streak is 29, set by Jesse Crain in 2013.</p><p>“It’s one of those things where you don’t try to think about it,” Hudson told the Sun-Times. “You just go in, do your routine and just get ready to pitch.”</p><p>That he has. The last time Hudson allowed a run was March 31 in Miami. Three days earlier, he allowed one in Milwaukee — and that’s it. In 20 innings covering 21 appearances, Hudson had a 0.90 ERA with 17 hits, nine walks and 22 strikeouts. His ERA is the lowest by a Sox pitcher in his first 21 outings of a season since Alex Colome had a 0.84 mark in 2020.</p><p>“We have a really good plan with the catchers,” Hudson said. “Me and the pitching coaches [Zach Bove and assistant Bobby Hearn] went over some stuff usage-wise, and we’re recognizing things that are working.</p><p>“The fastball’s been working, and then also the sweeper has been getting them off the heater and allowing me to get on them with the fastball.”</p><p>Hudson isn’t overpowering. His four-seam fastball has averaged 92 mph and his sweeper 81, but his movement has been deceptive.</p><p>Hudson is one of four Illinois natives on the Sox, along with right-hander reliever Trevor Richards (Aviston), left-handed starter Noah Schultz (Naperville) and outfielder Sam Antonacci (Springfield). His height landed him several scholarship offers to play basketball, but he stuck with baseball.</p><p>Growing up about 35 miles north of St. Louis, Hudson grew up as a Cardinals fan, thanks to his grandmother, Kim, who took him to games at the old and new Busch Stadium.</p><p>She altered her loyalty once the rival Cubs drafted Hudson.</p><p>“Obviously, it was a blessing [being drafted], no doubt,” Hudson said. “It was a big switch. My grandma was pretty much, Now I’m a Cardinals <i>and</i> a Cubs fan.”</p><p>Hudson could face the Cubs this weekend in the first round of the Crosstown Series at Rate Field. It wouldn’t be the first time. In his best big-league season, with the Brewers in 2024 (1.73 ERA in 43 games), he faced the Cubs five times in relief, allowing three runs in 7⅔ innings — and going 2-0.</p><p>He’ll be looking for more of that. His loyalty has changed, too.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Guilty verdict in 2021 Loop stabbing death of graduate student
entries.summary: <p>A jury of seven men and five women found Tony Robinson guilty late Thursday in the murder of graduate student Anat Kimchi, who was fatally stabbed in an unprovoked attack Downtown.</p><p>Robinson, 45, was charged with killing Kimchi by sneaking up on her and stabbing her three times in the neck and back. Jurors deliberated five hours before reaching their verdict.</p><p>In the gallery, Kimchi’s mother broke down in tears while relatives and friends comforted her. Both of Kimchi’s parents said they were too emotional in the moment to speak.</p><p>Robinson did not visibly react when the verdict was read aloud in court. He faces up 20 to 60 years in prison, prosecutors said. He will be sentenced July 8 in Cook County Circuit Judge John F. Lyke’s courtroom in the Leighton Criminal Courthouse</p><p>Kimchi, 31, a University of Maryland doctoral student, was killed June 19, 2021 in the 400 block of South Wacker Drive, just south of Van Buren Street. She was posthumously awarded her doctorate two weeks after her death.</p><p>Kimchi was in Chicago to visit a friend. It was a sunny Saturday afternoon, and she was walking just south of the Willis Tower, looking for a place to read a book.</p><p>While prosecutors did not have video evidence of the crime, and no weapon was recovered, they strove to connect the dots for jurors by playing multiple videos, recorded by surveillance cameras, showing Robinson's whereabouts around the time of the unprovoked attack.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-9b0000" name="image-9b0000"></a> <picture class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Shortly before the attack around 3:30 p.m., a video showed Kimchi walking south in the 400 block of South Wacker Drive while a man approaches her.</p><p>In another video from moments after the stabbing attack, a man prosecutors identified as Robinson can be seen running into the Lower Wacker Drive tunnel holding a knife. Robinson lived in a tent on Lower Wacker.</p><p>Another video then shows him throwing an object in the direction of the Chicago River.</p><p>Yet another video showed him taking off and discarding his black T-shirt in an alcove off Lower Wacker. Police recovered the shirt, which DNA testing showed was “850 septillion times” more likely to be Robinson’s than anyone else’s.</p><p></p><p>In their closing argument to jurors Thursday, prosecutors urged them to use common sense in evaluating the video evidence.</p><p>Assistant State’s Attorney Meredith Rudolfi told jurors the man seen on video running from the scene was Robinson, who was also videoed numerous times in the days before and after the killing — and was also on police body-camera footage when the cops identified him at his tent.</p><p>“None of this is a coincidence. It all adds up to one thing. He did it,” Rudolfi said.</p><p>She called it “a sneak attack” Kimchi “could not see coming.”</p><p>The random, unprovoked nature of the attack “is horribly sad," Assistant State’s Attorney Anna Sedelmaier told jurors. “We don’t know what was in his head."</p><p>Kimchi’s murder was one of several shocking cases examined in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/chicago-downtown-attacks-mental-health-system" >a Chicago Sun-Times investigation last year</a> into violent attacks Downtown.</p><p>According to police and court records, Robinson had a history of arrests and bizarre behavior, including telling detectives “he believes people are following him and tracking his location using their cellphones.”</p><p>In the days before Kimchi’s killing, authorities said Robinson struck a woman in the head in the 500 block of South Franklin Street and three days later hit another woman in the head, breaking her nose, and stole her iPhone and cash near Ida B. Wells Parkway and South Michigan Avenue. That woman told police she heard Robinson say, “Are you following me?” before the attack.</p><p>Tavon Jones, who was homeless at the time, testified he saw Robinson stab Kimchi in the back of the neck and ran over to try to stop the attack. Jones said Robinson turned to him and said, “You don’t want none of these problems, big bro.”</p><p>Jones said he saw Robinson flee toward Lower Wacker. Jones used Kimchi’s phone to call 911 and stayed with her until an ambulance and police arrived.</p><p>Jones failed to pick Robinson out of a photo array but later identified him as the killer in a live line-up.</p><p>The defense stressed that the live lineup identification came only after Jones had seen the photo array and then gone to Robinson’s tent to confront him, and they reminded jurors Jones’s initial description of the offender did not match Robinson.</p><p>During Thursday’s closing arguments, Robinson, dressed in a white button-down shirt, black pants and a white cap, mostly faced the jury and leaned back his his chair.</p><p>Earlier in the week, Kimchi’s mother, Chava Kimchi-Sarfaty, testified about how much she misses her daughter, a gifted researcher and animal lover.</p><p>Kimchi was drawn to psychology and criminal justice and earned two undergraduate degrees and a master’s from the University of Maryland in College Park before pursuing her doctorate.</p><p></p><p>Her research focus was on nonviolent offenders who wind up in prison after having their community supervision sentences revoked. Kimchi found significant differences in the severity of community supervision requirements among people of different races and ethnicities.<br></p>
